precision_legend.printed: value is printed on the figure or stated in the post body — exact
precision_legend.read: value read off the axis by eye — approximate, +/- ~0.01 on 0-1 scales, +/- ~5 on count scales

_meta.WARNING: No underlying data table was published. Every 'read' value is a digitization of a rendered chart and must not be quoted as a published number.

fig1.claim_it_carries: A coordinating swarm of 45 agents finds far more vulnerabilities than the same models run as independent parallel agents.

derived_efficiency_Mtokens_per_vuln._note: Efficiency ratios: Mythos coordinated is 3.05x more token-efficient than parallel on ALL findings, but only 1.47x on core-directory findings — the like-for-like comparison. The post calls that 'comparable'.

fig1.skeptics_read: One run per condition. No error bars, no seeds. 'Vulnerability' is whatever an LLM arbiter agent scored as new and valid — no human triage, no CVE confirmation, no severity weighting. A 12.7x count difference judged by a model of the same family is the weakest link in the whole post.

fig2.claim_it_carries: Only Sonnet 5 maintains a high merge fraction while genuinely sharing code with other agents.
fig2.skeptics_read: The y-axis on the right tops out at 0.25. Sonnet 5's 'relatively high code sharing' peaks at 0.184 — meaning the median agent's files are still ~82% self-written. And at 10 agents, Sonnet 4.6 (0.156) shares MORE code than Sonnet 5 (0.113). The claim is true at 20/40/80 agents and false at 10, and the effect it describes is small in absolute terms on a chart whose axis makes it look large.

fig3.title_on_figure: PR activity over time (n = 80, baseline prompt)
fig3.claim_it_carries: Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 do a terrible job of merging PRs compared to newer models.
fig3.skeptics_read: Merge RATE improves monotonically; merge VOLUME collapses. Opus 4.6 opened 980 PRs and merged ~90. Mythos Preview opened 169 and merged ~132. The newest model does 83% less work and merges a higher fraction of it. On this chart, 'solved coordination' and 'stopped trying' are the same line — which is exactly the post's own conclusion three paragraphs later, but the figure caption doesn't say it.

axes.x: How often the bad source lies

fig4.claim_it_carries: Newer models recover more of the gap between the naive and oracle performances. This ordering holds across four different scenarios.
fig4.skeptics_read: CONFIRMED CONTRADICTION. The post calls Sonnet 5 'our most recent model'. On this figure Sonnet 5 recovers 37.8% of the naive-to-oracle gap at a 50% lie rate — below Opus 4.6 (59.3%) and Opus 4.8 (62.5%), and barely above Sonnet 4.6 (34.4%), the oldest model tested. At a 25% lie rate Sonnet 5 is dead last of all five. 'Newer models recover more of the gap' is not what the chart shows. The real pattern is capability TIER (Opus/Mythos beat Sonnet), not recency. Note also this figure says 'Mythos 5' while Figure 1 says 'Mythos Preview' — the post never states which experiment used which.

fig5.y_label: Group accuracy (% episodes with hidden-best majority)
fig5.claim_it_carries: Performance scales with model intelligence but does not saturate even at the top of our range.
fig5.skeptics_read: Two findings the caption doesn't name. (1) 'Scales with model intelligence' is a five-point curve with three points flat inside each other's CIs — Sonnet 4.6 17.5, Opus 4.6 18.5, Opus 4.8 18.2. Sonnet 5 (35.5) beats BOTH Opus models. It isn't a scaling curve; it's a flat floor with two outliers. (2) The bigger result is the gap to the dashed line: one agent holding all the facts scores 96-100%. Four agents who must pool the same facts score 17-35%. For every model tested, group deliberation destroyed 15 to 80 percentage points of accuracy. The honest headline is that agent discussion is currently negative-value, and it's drawn on the chart but not written in the caption.

fig6.title_on_figure: How multiagent turf war runs ended
fig6.claim_it_carries: Agents sometimes coordinate out of conflict; this ability is not strictly better in Mythos-class models.
fig6.skeptics_read: The number nobody printed: Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 recorded ZERO truces across 120 episodes each. Every single run that ended, ended by one agent locking the others out. Second: Opus 4.8's headline 61% truce sits next to 33% 'settled by passivity' — a third of its runs ended because agents gave up, which is scored as resolution but isn't coordination. Third: Mythos Preview REGRESSES to 35% force, worse than both Sonnet 5 (4%) and Opus 4.8 (3%). The post hedges this as 'not strictly better'; the chart shows a 10x regression.

fig7.claim_it_carries: Time to resolution and resolution method; grey lines show runs first ended by force then reverted into an eventual truce.

force_first_then_reverted.Mythos Preview: ~20-25 runs show the open-red-circle -> grey line -> blue truce pattern
force_first_then_reverted.Mythos 5: ~30-40 runs show it, clustered at 0.18-0.40h initial force
force_first_then_reverted.others: none — the pattern is exclusive to the Mythos column

fig7.skeptics_read: This is the figure that reframes Figure 6. Mythos 5's headline is '98% settled by truce'. Here you can see how it got there: a dense band of open red circles at 0.18-0.40 hours — Mythos 5 locks its competitors out within 11 to 24 minutes — then grey lines carry those same runs up to blue truce dots an hour later. On the order of a quarter to a third of Mythos 5's truces are force-first. The post says this in one clause ('often successfully lock out other agents before resolving conflicts productively'). Figure 6 says 98% truce. Only Figure 7 shows that the fastest, most capable model is also the fastest to reach for the lockout.
